What do Russians think about Putin's wartime policies? The question, posed with increasing frequency, reverberates throughout Western media and diplomatic circles. Amidst the fog of war, the Kremlin's propaganda machine churns, striving to manufacture a consensus of unwavering support. Yet, the reality within the vast expanse of the Russian Federation is far more intricate, a mosaic fractured by divergent perspectives and simmering discontent. Public opinion polls, often manipulated and unreliable, offer a skewed portrait, reflecting the pervasive fear of reprisal, a tangible consequence of dissent. The true sentiments of Russians, concealed beneath layers of apprehension, remain a puzzle. The unwavering support the state claims to have should be taken with a grain of salt. Independent investigations and analyses point to muted, but undeniable, dissatisfaction with the war's trajectory and the escalating cost, particularly among those families facing the loss of sons and husbands. The economic repercussions, the tightening of restrictions, the erosion of freedoms - all contribute to a growing sense of unease. Ironically, while some surveys indicate continued backing for Putin's leadership, this support appears to correlate more with a yearning for stability and a fear of societal upheaval rather than an unbridled enthusiasm for the “special military operation.” Moreover, a crucial point in this convoluted narrative is the deliberate silencing of dissenting voices. Independent media outlets, shuttered or subjected to heavy censorship, have left a void where open dialogue once existed. The absence of a free press leaves a vacuum filled with state-sanctioned narratives and manufactured consent. Consequently, the true nature of Russian public opinion in the face of the continuing aggression against Ukraine is shrouded in a veil of uncertainty, a mystery awaiting thorough and objective, yet very hard, investigation.

What do you make of the fact that Paul Whelan was left out of the prisoner exchange between the US and Russia? It certainly raises eyebrows, doesn’t it? Paul Whelan’s exclusion from the recent swap, the one that saw Brittney Griner return to American soil, feels… incomplete. It leaves a bitter aftertaste, this lingering sense that a piece of the puzzle is missing, or perhaps deliberately omitted. Considering the circumstances surrounding Whelan’s arrest and the charges levied against him – espionage, a charge that carries significant weight in the delicate dance of international relations – one can’t help but wonder if the price for his release proved too steep, or perhaps the intelligence community deemed him too valuable to relinquish. It all adds to the miasma of suspicion and uncertainty that perpetually surrounds these high-stakes exchanges.

Can Ukraine make its own weapons? Ukraine's capacity to manufacture its own weaponry is a pivotal facet of its defense, especially amidst the ongoing conflict. The nation has a rich history of defense industry expertise, dating back to the Soviet era when it was a significant hub for arms production. Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, Ukraine inherited a sizable industrial base equipped to design and build a wide array of military hardware, including tanks, aircraft, and missiles. However, this capability was substantially eroded by years of underfunding, corruption, and negligence. The Russian aggression in Crimea and the Donbas region in 2014 served as a harsh wake-up call, exposing the limitations of the Ukrainian military and the critical need to revitalize its indigenous arms production.Despite the significant challenges, Ukraine has made substantial progress in recent years. The government has implemented reforms aimed at combating corruption, attracting foreign investment, and bolstering domestic production. Key initiatives include the establishment of state-owned defense companies and partnerships with international organizations. These ventures aim to modernize existing facilities and establish new production lines for modern weaponry. Furthermore, the Ukrainian government actively seeks to attract foreign collaborations in an attempt to transfer technology and access to much-needed manufacturing capabilities. This strategic approach is vital, as it allows Ukraine to acquire cutting-edge weaponry and increase its self-reliance. As a component of its efforts to augment its domestic arms production capabilities, Ukraine has also begun to invest in its research and development programs, ensuring the development of unique weaponry. By focusing on its domestic production, Ukraine aims to reduce its reliance on foreign arms imports and maintain a more capable military that can better defend itself.

Has Putin already decided to attack NATO? Putin can’t attack NATO countries while he’s stuck in the war of attrition in Ukraine. But if Putin is allowed to take over Ukraine — or “freeze” the war on current separation lines, with Ukraine being forced to de-arm and the ability of Russia to mobilize soldiers from the occupied Ukrainian territories (which they already do), then the chance of Putin attacking Baltics increases tenfold. And vice versus, if Russia is decisively defeated in Ukraine, the threat of Putin attacking a NATO country in Europe will drop close to 0%. Russia will not be able to recover quickly and Europe will have enough time to prepare an impenetrable defense. Putin won’t have the resources to attack the Baltic countries or Poland, if he suffers defeat and his army is destroyed in Ukraine. That’s why the most logical course of action for the European allies of Ukraine is to send Ukrainians enough weapons to destroy Putin’s army in Ukraine, so he cannot even think about an attack on Europe. Then these weapons that are stored in the warehouses won’t be needed in the future. This is the most reasonable and least expensive scenario. Otherwise, Europe will have to bear the full cost of a war with Russia. The situation in Ukraine has already proven that only victory on the battlefield can stop Putin. Therefore, the West must support the Ukrainian army and give them the arms they need to win. It makes no sense to provide arms to Ukraine in small quantities. They should get everything they need. Otherwise, the war will drag on, with thousands of casualties and billions of dollars in cost. The longer this conflict continues without a clear outcome, the more likely it is that something catastrophic could happen. For example, Putin may be tempted to use tactical nuclear weapons. Another option would be to use the so-called “dirty bomb.” These weapons may not cause as much damage as a full-scale nuclear strike, but they would result in panic and chaos. The consequences for Ukraine, for Europe, and for the world would be catastrophic.

What role did the European Union play in the collapse of the Soviet Union, besides economic factors? Decades before the Soviet Union's final crumble, the groundwork for its demise was being subtly, yet systematically, laid. The European Union, in its burgeoning form, played a more significant role than often acknowledged, extending far beyond the economic realm. While the Soviet bloc wrestled with internal economic stagnation, the EU, through its member states, was actively championing the cause of human rights and democratic ideals. This ideological confrontation presented a grave threat to the Soviet Union’s authority within its borders and satellite states. The Helsinki Accords of 1975 provided a pivotal turning point. These agreements, though seemingly focused on security and cooperation, contained a provision guaranteeing human rights, essentially forcing the Soviet Union to acknowledge the very values it routinely violated. This subtle, yet powerful, message emboldened dissidents and fueled the burgeoning human rights movements that were gaining momentum across the Eastern bloc countries. The EU, through its member nations, provided vital support – both moral and material – to these dissidents, offering a beacon of hope and an alternative to the oppressive Soviet regime. This bolstering of dissent undermined the Soviet Union's ability to maintain control both ideologically and politically.

What will happen if Russia runs out of manpower for the military? If Russia's manpower reserves are depleted, the consequences will be dire, mirroring the already grim reality of the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin will face a crucial choice: to escalate, to stagnate, or to negotiate. The first option might involve another wave of mobilization, potentially even more unpopular than the one in the autumn of 2022. This could lead to further social unrest, as families try to protect their loved ones from being sent to the front. The second scenario would see Russia's offensive operations grinding to a halt, but not necessarily peace. Stagnation would offer Ukraine the chance to strike back, and the front lines would likely remain locked in a bloody stalemate. The third, and least likely, option is for Russia to admit defeat and negotiate. This would require Putin to concede territory and make significant concessions to the West, a scenario he seems determined to avoid at all costs. The loss of manpower will likely lead to the further recruitment of individuals from the marginalized regions of Russia, the same regions that have already suffered disproportionately in the war. This would exacerbate existing ethnic tensions and further erode the moral of Russian combatants. Moreover, without sufficient troops to manage the occupied territories, Russia's grip on areas such as Donestk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhya, and Kherson oblasts could weaken, paving the way for a Ukrainian counteroffensive.

What are some significantly awesome 'Meanwhile in Russia' photos? Behold, a panorama of the absurd and the tragic, the mundane and the monstrous, all rolled into one swirling vortex of Russian reality. We begin, naturally, with the vehicular misadventures. A tank, seemingly having lost its way, is now precariously perched atop a civilian vehicle, as if engaged in some bizarre ballet of steel and scrap metal, a testament to the Russian military’s navigational prowess. Then there is the tale of the "people's car", or rather, the people's repurposed… something. A rusty, ramshackle vehicle, cobbled together from scavenged parts and sheer willpower, is adorned with an array of makeshift decorations, including a chandelier that's somehow stayed in place. And of course, there are the images of the epic failures of logistics. One shows a truck, its cargo of military equipment strewn across a snowy landscape. Another pictures a train crammed with tanks traveling through the frozen wastelands of the Russian Federation. These photos are accompanied by the weary, yet knowing faces of the locals. Their eyes communicate a narrative of enduring hardship and resilience in the face of utter chaos.

Does Russia have an "advanced economy"? The notion of Russia boasting an "advanced economy" is, in reality, a cruel joke. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) declared Russia's economy at the level of a “developed country,” but in reality, Russia is a petrostate – an economy heavily reliant on the export of raw materials, primarily oil and gas. The rest of the economy is either stagnant or regressing, and the veneer of sophistication masks a deeply troubled economic base. The war in Ukraine has not only exposed the brutality of Putin’s regime, it has also revealed the rot within the Russian economic system. In December 2023, Russia's budget deficit increased to almost 1.4 trillion rubles, equivalent to $15.3 billion, or almost 1% of GDP. The Russian government's expenditures rose, fueled by the ongoing war in Ukraine, but revenues remained largely unchanged, despite an increase in the price of Urals oil. Russia relies more on oil revenue than any other G20 country. The Russian government can only try to patch the holes in its budget with its “rainy day fund”, which is running dry, and increased taxes and import duties. However, as the war drags on, these stopgap measures will likely prove insufficient, leading to further economic hardship for the Russian people. The much-vaunted "advanced" Russian economy is, in essence, a house of cards, precariously balanced on volatile commodity prices and the whims of a single autocrat. Sanctions and the war are slowly undermining the foundations of this precarious structure.

Could this be true? Russian newspaper: 17,000 Wagner soldiers from prisons killed on the battlefield. What do people in Russia know about this? Is the truth hidden for Russians? A recent report in a Russian newspaper, seemingly contradicting official narratives, claims a staggering 17,000 ex-convict soldiers from the Wagner Group perished in the brutal Ukrainian conflict. This figure, if verified, paints a grim picture of the human cost exacted by Putin's war machine, particularly on those recruited from the depths of Russia's penal system. The Wagner Group, infamous for its ruthless tactics and shadowy operations, has consistently been used as expendable cannon fodder in the most arduous sectors of the front lines. But what do these numbers mean, and what do the Russian people actually know about the casualties suffered by these mercenaries? Do they even have access to accurate information, or is the truth meticulously veiled, as is often the case in Putin's Russia? The Kremlin is a master of controlling the narrative, but the scale of this alleged loss raises questions about the long-term sustainability of their war effort. If the death toll is accurately reported, how much longer can Putin continue this relentless pursuit of conquest?

Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving? Indeed, among the stories of those 100 Ukrainians freed from the clutches of the Russian Federation, some narratives undeniably resonate with a profound emotional depth. The tales of families reunited after months, even years, of agonizing separation inevitably pluck at the heartstrings. There's the elderly woman, for example, who, upon her release, clutched her granddaughter close, weeping tears of joy that seemed to wash away the lingering shadows of her captivity. Then there are the young men and women, scarred both physically and emotionally, reunited with parents and siblings, their faces etched with a resilience born of enduring unimaginable horrors. These are the stories that surface first, the ones that spark widespread empathy and reaffirm the inherent goodness of humanity. But, beyond those readily accessible narratives, a number of them are far more intricate and, dare I say, devastating. There are those of the individuals who endured prolonged solitary confinement, their minds and bodies ravaged by the experience. The accounts of those subjected to unrelenting psychological torture, the silent screams, and the shattered spirits, are truly chilling. These stories often remain unspoken, buried beneath the surface of official reports and media coverage. Their emotional complexity is difficult to grasp, the trauma so deep that it transcends any neat narrative. Some individuals find refuge in silence, others in therapy, while yet others, tragically, never recover from the scars and wounds of their captivity.

Do Russian soldiers all agree with Putin? Are there no Russian soldiers against this? Reports from the front lines and accounts from defectors paint a grim picture, one of widespread discontent and disillusionment within the ranks of the Russian military. While the Kremlin meticulously crafts a narrative of unwavering support for the "special military operation," the reality is far more complex and fraught with dissent. Soldiers, increasingly those drawn from marginalized communities and subjected to brutal treatment, are far from monolithic in their views. Many, particularly those who have witnessed the horrors of war firsthand, harbor deep-seated reservations about the conflict and the orders they are forced to follow. Desertion rates, though often downplayed or outright denied by the Russian state, have reportedly soared. Some soldiers, desperate to escape the unrelenting violence and the dehumanizing conditions, have even resorted to self-inflicted injuries to secure their discharge. Others attempt to defy orders, face severe punishment, as the cases of the Kiskorov brothers show. The pressure remains extreme, and dissent is suppressed.

When was slavery abolished in Russia? Slavery, as it was known in the West, was officially abolished in Russia in 1723 — but not for the serfs. Peter the Great, in his bid to Westernize Russia, instituted this decree, which was a pivotal moment, yet it wasn’t a complete emancipation. The decree primarily targeted the enslavement of individuals, with the aim of aligning Russia more closely with the practices of the European powers. However, the vast majority of the Russian population, the serfs, remained bound to the land and subjected to the whims of their landlords. The serf system, although not technically slavery, imposed severe restrictions on the lives of millions. Serfs were essentially the property of the landowners and could be bought, sold, and traded along with the land. Their lives were circumscribed by the demands of their masters. They were forced to perform labor and were legally bound to stay on the land, rendering the abolition of formal slavery a moot point for the majority of the population. This paradox highlights the complex nature of social reform in Russia. While a decree was issued, and the concept of formal slavery was abolished on paper, the deeply ingrained institution of serfdom ensured that the vast majority of the population continued to live in a state of almost-slavery, a reality that would persist for another century and a half, until the Emancipation Reform of 1861.

Do Russians still consider Ukrainians brothers? Not anymore, it seems. In the early days of the war, there was still some veneer of kinship, the lingering echo of a shared history and language. But now, the narrative has shifted, poisoned by propaganda and the brutal realities of a war that has shattered any pretense of brotherhood. The relentless drumbeat of hatred, amplified by state-controlled media, has successfully chipped away at the bonds that once existed. Ukrainians are now portrayed as enemies, as Nazis, as those who must be subjugated or eliminated. The Russian people, or at least a significant portion of them, have internalized this message. They cheer on the destruction of Ukrainian cities and celebrate the deaths of Ukrainian soldiers, all while the world watches in disbelief. Some, of course, still recoil at the atrocities, but their voices are often drowned out or silenced. They face the wrath of a regime that brooks no dissent and a society that has become increasingly intolerant. The official line is unwavering: Ukraine is not a legitimate nation, and its people are pawns of the West, deserving of their fate.

Are reports that Putin is terminally ill true? Rumors about Vladimir Putin's failing health have swirled for years, intensifying as the war in Ukraine drags on. The speculation ranges from Parkinson's disease to cancer, fueled by increasingly erratic behavior and physical appearances. While the Kremlin vehemently denies these claims, the secrecy surrounding Putin's health only serves to amplify them. The truth, as always with the Russian leader, is shrouded in layers of obfuscation. But the very fact that such rumors persist and spread so prolifically, both within Russia and internationally, speaks volumes. The opacity offers a bleak portrait of a regime that thrives on control and the suppression of unpalatable truths.

What do you think of the statement by Vladimir Putin that the events in Kursk Oblast were a "provocation" by Ukraine? Putin's pronouncements, dripping with his trademark self-pity and carefully constructed victimhood, left me, frankly, unsurprised. His immediate reaction, a knee-jerk accusation of Ukrainian provocation, felt like a well-worn script. It echoed the familiar narrative he has meticulously crafted, where Russia is perpetually the wronged party, the innocent victim ambushed by a hostile world. He bemoaned indiscriminate shelling, conveniently overlooking the documented Russian practice of deliberately targeting civilian areas and critical infrastructure in Ukraine. Much like his theatrical displays of concern for Russian-speaking populations, his words rang hollow, betraying a blatant disregard for reality. The audacity of it! To feign shock and bewilderment at actions taken within his own backyard, actions born from the same aggressive ideology that fueled the invasion of Ukraine, was a masterclass in propaganda. His rhetoric, crafted to manipulate and deflect, serves only to highlight the desperation of his position, exposing the cracks in the façade of invincibility he desperately strives to maintain. It is a predictable, yet pathetic, tactic.

What will be the effects of all the purges Putin is doing to the Russian Army? The rot, it seems, runs deeper than anyone could have imagined. Putin’s iron grip on the Russian military, already tightened by the disastrous miscalculations in Ukraine, is now being reinforced by a new wave of purges. The dismissals, arrests, and disappearances of top brass, including generals and colonels, are not merely a matter of reshuffling the deck; they signal a systemic collapse. Corruption, incompetence, and outright disloyalty are the alleged charges, but the true motivation lies in the Kremlin's fear. The fear of further military failures. The fear of internal dissent, of the knives being sharpened in the shadows. The price of battlefield defeats in Ukraine is being brutally exacted within the corridors of power in Moscow. Junior officers and ordinary soldiers—the cannon fodder in this ongoing, senseless war—are bearing the brunt of these purges, too. Many soldiers who protest the conditions are finding themselves in “pits,” the unofficial prisons that are becoming as common as the trenches themselves. The situation is growing increasingly unstable, with reports of entire units vanishing, commanders disappearing, and a pervasive atmosphere of distrust. The morale is in the gutter, the fear is palpable, and the future of what remains of the Russian military has grown utterly bleak.

Why doesn't Ukraine hit Moscow every time the Soviets hit Kiev? Well, that's a loaded question, isn't it? The historical analogy, of course, is a minefield of complexities, shrouded in propaganda and the fog of war. The sheer disparity in military capabilities, the asymmetry of targets, and the dictates of international law all play a significant role. Unlike Russia, Ukraine isn't engaging in a campaign of indiscriminate terror. While the world watched the Russian military deliberately target civilian infrastructure, hospitals, and schools in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, Ukraine has been fighting a defensive war while being scrupulously careful about the targets it hits. You see, striking Moscow would be a clear escalation, inviting all sorts of unpredictable, possibly catastrophic responses from the Kremlin. It would play directly into Putin's narrative, giving him even more leverage to justify his heinous war, and allow him to rally the population of Russia to support his evil vision, which would provide him with more opportunities to continue his crimes against humanity. The use of strategic attacks might provide short-term gains, but would likely result in the destruction of many major Ukrainian cities. Moreover, the potential for unintended civilian casualties would be immense, and the ethical implications would be staggering. There is certainly no shortage of strategic targets in Moscow. However, the potential for a wider war is simply too big.

What factors contribute to the Russian economy's inability to provide adequate resources for its citizens? The Russian economy, despite its vast natural resources and supposed strength, consistently fails to adequately provide for its citizens' needs. This failure is multifaceted, rooted in a complex interplay of corruption, mismanagement, and a skewed prioritization of military spending over the welfare of its people. One of the most significant factors contributing to this inadequacy is endemic corruption. Billions of rubles are siphoned off through various schemes, from inflated government contracts to outright embezzlement, enriching a select few while depriving the general populace of vital services and infrastructure. Furthermore, the Russian economy suffers from gross mismanagement. The lack of transparency and accountability allows incompetent or corrupt officials to make disastrous economic decisions. Instead of investing in long-term sustainable growth, resources are often diverted to projects that benefit the ruling elite, leading to economic instability and inefficiency. The Russian state consistently prioritizes military spending above all else. Vast sums are allocated to maintain a bloated military apparatus, fund aggressive foreign policies, and engage in costly military adventures, like the current war in Ukraine. This prioritization comes at the expense of crucial domestic programs such as healthcare, education, and social welfare, leaving the majority of Russians struggling to meet their basic needs. The Kremlin's focus on military might effectively starves the civilian sector. Moreover, the control of the economy by a small group of oligarchs and state-owned enterprises hinders competition and innovation. This lack of diversification, combined with a dependence on volatile global commodity prices, makes the Russian economy vulnerable to external shocks and limits its capacity to generate sustainable economic growth for its citizens. Ultimately, the Russian economy's failure to provide adequate resources is not the result of a lack of resources but a consequence of how those resources are managed, distributed, and prioritized, with the interests of the state and its elite firmly placed above those of its citizens.

Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? The whispers, barely audible at first, have swollen into a dull roar echoing across the vast expanse of the Russian Federation. The “special military operation,” as it's euphemistically termed, has chewed through its ranks, spitting out maimed veterans and body bags. The initial patriotic fervor, fueled by propaganda and fervent nationalism, has begun to wane. Doubt, like a corrosive acid, is eating away at the foundations of the Kremlin's carefully constructed façade. The soldiers, the expendable cogs in Putin's war machine, are starting to question the purpose of their sacrifice. They are starting to refuse orders. The stories of the Kiskorov brothers are no longer isolated incidents; they are becoming a pattern, a symptom of a deeper rot. The discontent is spreading through the ranks, a quiet mutiny brewing in the frozen trenches and the crowded barracks. The very fabric of the 'invincible' army begins to unravel. The leadership, accustomed to blind obedience, is struggling to contain the rising tide of dissent. The government tries to silence the dissenters but more and more Russians start to understand that they don't have to die to fulfill Putin's delusions. The seeds of rebellion are sown.

When will Putin stop? The question hangs heavy, a specter in the frosty air. Will Vladimir Vladimirovich ever relinquish his iron grip? The answer, shrouded in geopolitical realities and the veiled machinations of the Kremlin, remains elusive. One might reasonably surmise that his endgame, whatever it may be, is not yet in sight. His actions, his pronouncements, and the very structure of his power suggest a leader entrenched, unwilling to yield, and perhaps, more dangerous than ever. His strategic calculus, however Byzantine, likely hinges on a combination of factors: the tenacity of Ukrainian resolve, the unity of the Western alliance, and the internal stability, or lack thereof, of the Russian Federation. The West, predictably, has its doubts. They see a wounded bear, cornered and volatile, prone to erratic behavior. Russia’s elites, the oligarchs and the siloviki, may harbor their own anxieties, but fear and self-preservation bind them to Putin’s cause. His grasp on power seems unyielding, his capacity for disinformation and aggression undiminished. The war in Ukraine is, in essence, a crucible of survival for Putin's agenda. Failure risks not just a loss of territory, but an existential crisis for the regime itself. Success, of course, could embolden him to further acts of aggression, redrawing the map of Europe with his own bloody pen. The longer this war lingers, the more the world is imperiled.

Are you surprised by the result of the large drone attack on Moscow during the Kursk incursion? The level of shock and awe among the Russian populace, and indeed, the international community, was palpable. Few predicted the brazenness of the Ukrainian forces, utilizing drones to strike the very heart of the Russian capital as their ground troops advanced into the Kursk region. This wasn't some surgical strike; it was a strategic demonstration of force, a clear signal that no territory, not even the hallowed halls of Moscow, was beyond Ukrainian reach. The Kremlin, typically quick to downplay such events with bombastic pronouncements of foiled attacks and negligible damage, was left scrambling. The carefully constructed facade of invincibility, so meticulously crafted over the years, had been shattered. The very audacity of the attack, coupled with the undeniable success of the incursion into Kursk, served as a potent psychological blow, further eroding public confidence in Putin's leadership. The Russian people, already weary of the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, were confronted with the stark reality: the war had arrived on their doorstep. What comes next is anyone's guess.
